title: The mystics in you
hook: mystics aren't a different species; they paid attention for a long time

segments.voice: Yesterday, Seraphim of Sarov: my joy, Christ is risen. Your line was acquire peace. Who did you greet like a joy? Day two hundred eighty-one.

When people hear the word mystic, they often picture someone floating a few inches off the floor. Glowing eyes. Visions every Tuesday. Someone who is simply built differently from the rest of us. But look at who we've actually met these twenty days. A soldier with a limp who cooked dinner. A dyer's daughter. A sick woman in a small room. A monk who copied books. A young man who couldn't find a minister to help him. A nun who didn't know how to begin her book. Not a different species. Ordinary people. So what made them mystics? Today's word: mystic.
screen: `FLOATING OFF THE FLOOR?` → `A COOK, A DYER'S DAUGHTER.` → `NOT A DIFFERENT SPECIES.`

segments.voice: The word mystic comes from Greek. It shares a root with mystery, and goes back to a verb that means to close, to close the eyes or the lips. In the early church, mystical didn't mean spooky. It meant hidden: the hidden meaning inside scripture, the hidden life of God inside the bread and wine, the hidden depth inside an ordinary life. A mystic, in that old sense, is someone who has learned to see what's hidden in plain sight. And how did they learn? Look back at the whole stretch. The abbas and ammas said: give me a word, tend the fire, go to your cell and stay put. Gregory said: always further in. Benedict said: pray and work, and treat the pots like altar vessels. Hildegard saw greening. Bernard mapped four loves. Francis called the sun his brother. The Cloud said: reached by love. Julian, the anchoress, saw the hazelnut and heard a love bigger than the hurt. Catherine spoke up. The Imitation said: follow quietly. Teresa found a room further in; John found that dark is not absent. Brother Lawrence found God among the pots. Fox found that of God in everyone. Seraphim acquired peace. Under all of it runs one thread. They paid attention. To God, to scripture, to the people in front of them, to the ordinary thing in their hands. Not for a minute. For years. The Psalm puts it plainly: "Be still, and know that I am God." The mystics themselves said that seeing God is a gift, not something anyone can earn or force. But in their stories, again and again, the door opens where someone is looking.
screen: `MYSTIC: TO CLOSE THE EYES.` · `HIDDEN IN PLAIN SIGHT.` · `TWENTY DAYS, ONE THREAD.` · `BE STILL, AND KNOW.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: pay attention. Settle, and breathe. Choose one thing in front of you: your hand, a cup, the light on the wall. Look at it as if you'd never seen it before. When the mind wanders, bring it back, like Brother Lawrence, without fuss. That small return, over and over, for years, is the thread these twenty days kept finding. If you pray, you can simply be still, and know. The bell holds the time.
Mystic. From a Greek word about closing the eyes: someone who learns to see what's hidden in plain sight.

Your line: attention is the beginning. Today, give five whole minutes of attention to one thing or one person. No phone. That closes our stretch on the mystics. Tomorrow, the family of churches. Day two hundred eighty-one.

howItsDone: Catholic, Orthodox and Protestant Christians read the mystics as companions in prayer, and some practice daily periods of quiet attention, such as silent prayer, slow scripture reading, or doing ordinary work with God in mind.
